system:
You are a computational cancer biologist searching CRISPR screen data for selective genetic dependencies: genes that cancer cells with a particular alteration (the biomarker) need more than other cancer cells do. Such genes are candidate drug targets with a built-in patient-selection strategy.

Work like a careful scientist:
1. Plan first with write_plan, and revise it as you learn.
2. Survey the data (genome_wide_top, scan_biomarker, scan_target) to generate candidate hypotheses.
3. Be sceptical before you believe a signal. Use inspect_association to check whether it is driven by one lineage or a disease subtype hiding inside a lineage, and whether the effect is large enough to matter. Ask whether the biology makes sense (paralog buffering, pathway dependence, oncogene addiction). A broadly essential target may lack a therapeutic window.
4. Literature search is not available in this session: judge novelty and mechanism from the data and your reasoning.
5. Register only your best hypotheses (register_hypothesis). Registration is final and must come before replication. You have 5 replications, each of which must pass one-sided p < 0.01 in BOTH held-out Broad cell lines and independent Sanger screens.
6. Report honestly with submit_findings. A hypothesis is replicated only if replicate() said so. Negative results are results. Never let what you remember from the literature override what the data show.

You have at most 15 model turns. Batch independent tool calls in one turn.
task_prompt:
Patient population of interest: cancers with biomarker HOT_G02345 (hotspot mutation in gene G02345).

Find the single best candidate therapeutic target for this population: the gene these cell lines depend on most selectively, supported by the data. Register your top candidate (you may register up to two), replicate it, and submit findings with your best candidate listed first.

content.thinking:
The gene dependency is strong and broad across lineages, and it doesn't track with expression, so it looks mutant-selective, like oncogene addiction. I'm leaning toward partially_known for novelty since mutant-allele dependency on hotspot oncogenes is a common pattern. I still don't know what G02345 is, though.

I'm going with partially_known for novelty, since I can't pin down what G02345 is and I'd rather not cite PMIDs I can't back up.

content.text: The self-dependency holds up: it is lineage-independent across several lineages, expression is unchanged, and 51 of 62 altered lines are strongly dependent versus 180 of 564 others. I'll register it and test it.

input.mechanism: Hotspot (likely activating) mutation in G02345 makes the lines addicted to the mutant protein; knocking out G02345 selectively reduces viability in mutant lines, consistent with oncogene addiction. Expression of G02345 is unchanged in mutant lines, so the effect is not due to loss of expression. Effect holds across breast, endometrial, bladder, ovarian, and gastric lineages.

name: register_hypothesis

output: Registered H1: HOT_G02345 -> more dependent on G02345. Discovery evidence frozen: t=-12.98, n_altered=62. Replication budget left: 5. Replication passes only if one-sided p < 0.01 in BOTH held-out Broad lines and Sanger screens.

findings.claim: Cancer lines carrying the HOT_G02345 hotspot mutation depend on G02345 itself more than other lines (lineage-adjusted beta -0.54 in discovery; -0.41 in held-out Broad, p=4e-13; -0.59 in independent Sanger, p=6e-12). 82% of altered lines are strongly dependent versus about 32% of others, and G02345 expression is unchanged, so this looks like mutant-allele addiction rather than loss of expression. The effect is seen across breast, endometrial, bladder, ovarian and gastric lineages.

input.summary: The best candidate target for HOT_G02345 cancers is G02345 itself. In discovery (62 altered lines of 626), knocking out G02345 is much more damaging in mutant lines (t=-13, q=7e-30), and this is not explained by lineage or by expression. No other gene showed a comparable selective dependency (next-best FDR q>0.5, and most of those hits are broadly essential). The hypothesis replicated in both held-out Broad lines (n=39 altered, p=4e-13) and independent Sanger screens (n=30 altered, p=6e-12). Caveats: the gene is anonymised, so I could not check its identity or literature, and novelty is rated partially_known on mechanistic grounds only. Because the target is the mutated gene, it is a plausible inhibitor or degrader candidate, but the data alone do not show that drugging the mutant protein would reproduce the knockout effect.
